title: Audio Fundamentals — Waveforms, Sampling, Fourier Transform

questions.question: A mono recorder samples at 48,000 samples per second for 2 seconds. How many waveform values does it store?
questions.explanation: At 48,000 samples per second × 2 seconds, a mono waveform stores 96,000 samples; mono has one stream, so there is no channel multiplier. The 24,000-sample option divides rate by duration, while the 48,000-sample option counts only one second.

questions.question: A signal is sampled at 10 kHz. What is its Nyquist frequency?
questions.explanation: Nyquist is half the sampling rate, so 10 kHz ÷ 2 = 5 kHz; frequencies above that boundary can alias into lower ones. The 10 kHz option repeats the sampling rate, while 20 kHz doubles it instead of taking half.

questions.question: For N = 256 samples at sr = 8,000 Hz, what frequency does DFT bin k = 14 represent?
questions.explanation: The bin spacing is sr/N = 8,000/256 = 31.25 Hz, so bin 14 represents 14 × 31.25 = 437.5 Hz. The 31.25 Hz option is adjacent-bin spacing, not bin 14; 875 Hz uses N = 128 rather than 256.

questions.question: Before decimating audio to a lower sample rate, what operation protects it from aliasing?
options: Convert the waveform from floats into signed integers
Apply a Fourier transform to the complete recording once
Low-pass filter frequencies beyond the new Nyquist limit
Normalize the waveform to unit peak amplitude
questions.explanation: Downsampling lowers the new Nyquist limit, so low-pass filtering must remove frequencies the target rate cannot represent before decimation. An FFT only analyzes the signal; it does not remove out-of-band energy, which otherwise folds into lower frequencies.

questions.question: A model expects 16 kHz mono audio, but a WAV is 44.1 kHz stereo. What should the loader do first?
options: Drop one channel and leave the samples at 44.1 kHz
Convert to 16-bit PCM and preserve both channels
Resample to 16 kHz and provide a mono waveform
Keep 44.1 kHz and relabel the header as 16 kHz
questions.explanation: A 16 kHz mono model expects samples on that clock and one channel, so resample and downmix the waveform before feature extraction. Changing metadata leaves sample spacing unchanged, while dropping a channel alone still leaves the sample-rate mismatch.

questions.question: For speech sampled at 16 kHz, which frame sizes implement a 25 ms window and a 10 ms hop?
questions.explanation: At 16 kHz, a 25 ms window is 0.025 × 16,000 = 400 samples, and a 10 ms hop is 0.010 × 16,000 = 160 samples. The 160-sample-window/400-sample-hop option reverses the two values; 800/80 instead means 50 ms and 5 ms.
